problems.reason: Three questions worth 20 of 100 points, including one of the two open-ended items, test the scientific method and the three domains from section 1.1, which no learning objective names, while unit conversion and Fahrenheit conversion get no questions.

problems.reason: Most items can be answered from memory: Questions 1, 4, 9, 12 and 13 ask for a definition or unit name, and Questions 2, 11, 14 and 15 reuse the source's own milk, rust, water and archery-target examples, although the objectives ask students to classify, apply and calculate.

problems.reason: The keyed option reaches 3.9 g/mL for a wrong reason, since division does not always limit results to two significant figures; the limit here comes from 3.2 mL having the fewest significant figures.

problems.assessment_text: $298.15\text{ K}$ because $273.15$ is added to Celsius
problems.source_text: When adding or subtracting numbers, round the result to the same number of decimal places as the number
problems.reason: 25.0 °C has one decimal place, so by the source's addition rule the kelvin value should be 298.2 K, and the keyed 298.15 K overstates the precision.

problems.source_text: lead 11.3 g/cm3
problems.reason: Unlike options A and B (mass divided by the final or the initial volume), 14 g/cm3 matches no likely calculation slip and does not match lead's 11.3 g/cm3, so choosing it reveals nothing about the student's thinking.

problems.assessment_text: An intensive property of matter is one that is independent of the ____ of matter present.
problems.source_text: independent of the amount of the substance
problems.reason: Words such as 'quantity' fill the blank just as correctly, but only 'amount' is keyed, so correct answers may be marked wrong.
